group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by her partner late this afternoon after three days of progressive shortness of breath and a new productive cough that yielded thick yellow sputum beginning yesterday evening; she reports that earlier today even slow conversation left her winded and she felt “light-headed” when walking from the bedroom to the kitchen. Home medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, low-dose furosemide taken most mornings for ankle swelling, aspirin 81 mg, and atorvastatin 40 mg at night. She was diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction two years ago after an admission for pulmonary edema, and an outpatient echocardiogram six months ago noted an ejection fraction of 30 %. Ten years earlier she suffered a left frontal ischemic stroke that left only a subtle right-hand clumsiness without speech or cognitive deficits; she completes crossword puzzles daily and drives herself to the grocery store once a week. She denies any chronic kidney disorder, has never required dialysis, and recalls her most recent creatinine being “around one.” There is no history of chronic liver problems, cancer, or residence in an extended-care facility; she and her partner live independently in a single-story home, climb the eight porch steps without assistance, and handle all activities of daily living themselves. She quit cigarette smoking 18 years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks wine once or twice a month, and has never used illicit substances. Vaccination records show receipt of both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza injection. Prior to arrival she took her usual morning medicines and a single 500 mg acetaminophen tablet but no diuretic beyond her routine dose, no antibiotics, steroids, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen. In triage, before any therapeutic intervention, she was seated upright, conversing in full sentences, and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Vital signs recorded an oral temperature of 37.7 °C, regular pulse 95 beats per minute, blood pressure 99/58 mm Hg confirmed by manual reading, respiratory rate 39 breaths per minute with shallow accessory muscle use, and pulse oximetry 83 % on ambient air that improved only to 86 % when she was asked to purse-lip breathe. Mucous membranes were dry, jugular venous pulsation was difficult to appreciate with the head of bed at 30°, and mild bilateral ankle pitting edema to 2 mm was present—unchanged from her baseline, according to the patient. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid but regular S1 and S2 with a faint third heart sound similar to prior clinic notes, no new murmurs or rubs. Pulmonary examination produced coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower posterior chest with dullness to percussion in that area, while the remainder of the fields were vesicular without wheeze; there was no stony dullness, egophony, or asymmetry of diaphragmatic motion to suggest fluid accumulation. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended; the liver edge was not palpable below the costal margin. Neurologic screening demonstrated equal and reactive pupils, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 motor strength except for slightly slowed rapid fine movements of the right hand, and unremarkable sensation, coordination, and gait (tested briefly with assistance). Capillary finger-stick glucose measured 107 mg/dL. Venous and arterial samples were obtained within ten minutes of arrival prior to fluids, diuretics, vasodilators, or antimicrobials. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 98 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, glucose 107 mg/dL (matching the point-of-care value), blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Hemogram showed hematocrit 54 % with hemoglobin 18.0 g/dL and white blood cell count 14.0 × 10⁹/L predominated by neutrophils; platelets were 260 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas obtained while she remained on room air demonstrated pH 7.53, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, PaO₂ 57 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and lactate 1.4 mmol/L, consistent with primary respiratory alkalosis accompanying significant hypoxemia. Upright posteroanterior and lateral chest radiographs obtained immediately thereafter revealed a dense consolidation filling the right lower lobe with air bronchograms; the heart was mildly enlarged but unchanged from prior films, the mediastinum midline, costophrenic angles sharp, and no layering fluid or meniscus sign was visualized. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 96 bpm with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria but no acute ischemic ST-T changes. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, urinary antigens for common bacterial pathogens, and a respiratory viral panel were sent to the laboratory. At the moment this note was completed, the patient had not received intravenous crystalloids, vasoactive agents, supplemental oxygen beyond brief pulse-oximetry measurement on room air, bronchodilators, diuretics, or antibiotics, ensuring that the physiologic and laboratory data detailed above reflect her untreated state at presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a 69-year-old woman starts at age minus 10 = 59. No nursing-home residence → 0.
- Comorbidities: heart failure → 10; prior ischemic stroke (cerebrovascular disease) → 10. No neoplasm, liver disease, or chronic renal disease → 0. Subtotal = 20.
- Examination: respiratory rate 39/min (≥30) → 20. She was oriented, systolic BP was 99 mmHg (not <90), temperature was 37.7°C (not <35 or ≥40), and pulse was 95/min (not ≥125) → 0 each. Subtotal = 20.
- Labs and imaging: BUN 36 mg/dL (≥30) → 20; sodium 126 mEq/L (<130) → 20; room-air PaO₂ 57 mmHg (<60) → 10. The low oxygen saturation is not scored again. Arterial pH 7.53 (not <7.35), glucose 107 mg/dL (not ≥250), hematocrit 54% (not <30%), and no pleural effusion → 0 each. Subtotal = 50.
Total = 59 + 20 + 20 + 50 = 149 (risk class V).
Final answer: 149
